# Introduction

Understanding what drives community assembly has been a central goal of ecology for a long time [@hillerislambers_rethinking_2012; @diamond_assembly_1975; @weiher_community_1998]. Not taking dispersal limitations into account, community composition is thought to be shaped by environmental constraints, competition, neutral processes, or a combination of all three [@gotzenberger_ecological_2012]. Investigating the functional trait patterns in communities offers insight into the dominant assembly processes at work in a community, and which environmental factors most strongly shape community composition [@ackerly2007; @gotzenberger_ecological_2012]. Environmental conditions are hypothesised to act as a filter, excluding species which may be able to disperse to a site but not survive there [@gotzenberger_ecological_2012; @kraft_community_2015]. This should create a pattern of trait convergence toward an optimum trait for survival [@gotzenberger_ecological_2012]. Competition is expected to promote divergence of functional traits under the theory of coexistence by niche differentiation [@weiher_community_1998]. However, competition may also generate a pattern of trait convergence if species with traits conferring higher competitive ability exclude species with weakly competitive traits [@mayfield2010].

The importance of limiting similarity and environmental filtering in structuring communities are expected to vary along stress gradients. Competition is expected to play a larger role in structuring communities in less stressful or high resource environments, while environmental filtering is predicted to be more important in abiotically harsh environments [@weiher_community_1998; @grime1977]. This idea has been pervasive in community ecology for a long time, but has been referred to as the stress dominance hypothesis (SDH) in recent years [@swenson2007; @coyle2014]. Support for this hypothesis is mixed. For example, convergence of SLA and seed mass increased with elevation in the Gaudarrama mountains [@pescador_spatial_2021], and the assembly of height and leaf area shifted from limiting similarity to environmental filtering with elevation in the Rocky mountains [@spasojevic2012]. However, specific leaf area, stomatal conductance, and chlorophyll content showed increased divergence along the same elevation gradient in the Rocky mountains [@spasojevic2012]. Other studies found no changes in assembly mechanisms along stress gradients, for example, along an aridity gradient in the Atacama desert [@carvajal2023], along gradients of soil water and nutrient availability [@coyle2014], and along an elevation gradient in the Swiss Alps [@scherrer_disentangling_2019].

Micro-environmental conditions are an additional, complex variable that may cause trends in community assembly to deviate from the expectations of the SDH. The importance of micro-environmental conditions in affecting community composition has gained recognition in recent years [@kemppinen_microclimate_2024; @vernham_understanding_2023], but the specific effect on community assembly processes has not been investigated extensively. Micro-environmental conditions may pose an additional filter, selecting species with optimum traits adapted to local micro-environmental conditions [@bergholz2017]. It follows that micro-environmental heterogeneity may promote the coexistence of species with divergent functional traits[@bergholz2017]. Thus, high micro-environmental heterogeneity may generate a pattern of trait divergence, even in stressful conditions. For example, mean moisture and temperature conditions within a 10m transect had a filtering effect on leaf area and plant height, but was related to divergence in LDMC [@stark2017]. Heterogeneity of temperature and moisture conditions within the transect was related to divergence in height and LDMC [@stark2017]. However, many studies find that plant communities follow neutral dynamics at fine scales (refs), or that there is little variation community assembly with micro-environmental variation [@aiello-lammens2017].

Here we will investigate the effect of an elevation gradient (macroclimate gradient) and micro-environmental condition son community assembly in a montane grassland. Macroclimate expected to influence assembly as predicted by the SDH. Micro-environment is predicted to...

Research questions: How does community assembly change with elevation?

Does fine-scale environmental heterogeneity influence community assembly?

# Methods

## Study site

Species composition, functional trait and micro-environmental data were collected from three study sites spread over an elevation gradient spanning 1000 m in the Northern Maloti-Drakensberg. The Maloti-Drakensberg is the highest extension of the great escarpment of South Africa, formed during the Jurassic period when outflows of basaltic lava covered sedimentary rocks of the Karoo supergroup [@knight2015]. The Maloti-Drakensberg is the only mountain range south of Kilimanjaro with an alpine zone [@kotze2023], with its highest peak reaching 3482 m a.s.l. The Maloti-Drakensberg falls within the grassland biome of South Africa [@mucina2006], where Poaceae species dominate in terms of cover and biomass. Herbaceous forbs have low cover but contribute the most to species richness, and woody shrubs or trees are sparse. The vegetation in the Maloti-Drakensberg is highly diverse, forming the Drakensberg Mountain Centre of endemism with a 9% plant endemism rate [@carbutt2019].

The study sites are located in the Golden Gate Highlands National Park (low site) at 2000 m a.s.l., Wistieshoek (mid site) at 2500 m a.s.l. and the Bokong Nature Reserve (high site) at 3000 m a.s.l (@fig-sitemap). The low site falls within the Northern Drakensberg Highland Grassland vegetation type [@mucina2006], characterised by taller, C4 grasses, and the presence of some trees such as *Protea* species, *Leucosidea sericea* and *Buddleja* species. The mid site falls within the uKahlamba Basalt grassland vegetation type [@mucina2006], which includes many C3 grass genera such as *Festuca*, *Pentameris* and *Tenaxia*, and a very high diversity of forbs. The high site is in the Lesotho Highland Basalt grassland vegetation type [@mucina2006], where the grass is extremely short and dominated by C3 species. Shrubs of e.g., *Erica* and *Passerina* are present, as well as cushion forming *Helichrysum* shrubs.

The climate in the Northern Maloti-Drakensberg is characterised by highly seasonal rainfall, with 75% of annual rainfall occurring in the summer months between November and March [@nel2009]. Mean annual rainfall typically ranges between 750 mm and 1350 mm, and occurs in the form of thunderstorms formed through orographic lift [@nel2009]. The total annual rainfall at the three sites are approximately 1310 mm p.a. at the low site, 1558 mm p.a. at the mid site, and 913 mm p.a. at the high site (total rainfall measured between 22/05/2025 and 21/05/2026 by the nearest weather stations of the African Mountain Research Foundation). Very little rainfall occurs in the winter (10mm - 190mm), but precipitation may also occur in the form of snow [@mulder2009]. Snow occurs when cold fronts or cutoff low pressure cells move over the Drakensberg [@mulder2009], and tends to melt before the next cold weather system arrives. Summer temperatures are mild, but winters are cold, with minimum temperatures regularly dropping below freezing [@nel2008]. Mean annual air temperature is 12℃ at the low site, 10℃ at the mid site and 7℃ at at the high site (mean daily temperature between 22/05/2025 and 21/05/2026 measured by the nearest weather stations of the African Mountain Research Foundation). Fires are a natural occurrence in the Maloti-Drakensberg, and are essential for the maintenance of plant biodiversity [@morris2021]. The majority of species in Drakensberg grasslands posses underground storage organs or bud banks from which they resprout after fire. Historically, fires were ignited by lightning and occurred in the early spring [@finch2022]. Since European occupation in the Drakensberg and surrounding area, fires tend to occur earlier, in the winter period [@finch2022].

The low site is formally conserved as a National Park where livestock has been excluded, but with large herbivores like zebra, blue wildebeest and eland present at the site. The mid site is situated on land owned by the Batlokoa Royal House, where livestock is not excluded but were never observed grazing at the mid site. Wild herbivores and omnivores such as grey rhebuck, klipspringer and baboon have been observed at the mid site. The high site is situated in the Bokong Nature Reserve managed by the National Government of Lesotho. Livestock is not permitted inside the reserve but herds have been observed passing through on their way to grazing pastures. Grey rhebuck, ice rat and rock hyrax are present at the high site. All three sites were located on basaltic bedrock, and were subject to a similar fire regime consisting of incidental wildfires started by lightning or accidental ignition.

At each site, species composition and functional traits were sampled using a grid design (@fig-sitemap c). Each grid was 8 x 20 m in size, consisting of 160 contiguous 1 x 1 m cells. Eight grids were sampled at the low site, and seven were sampled at the mid and high site (@fig-sitemap b). The grids were spaced \> 80 m apart in each site and were positioned to encompass the full range of environmental conditions at the site, covering a range of topographies and vegetation characteristics. In addition, individual grids were oriented to capture as much local variation in vegetation and topography as possible. This sampling design has previously been applied in high-altitude and high-latitude systems to sample broad environmental gradients and allows the influence of fine-scale heterogeneity to be examined without the confounding effect of macroclimate or species pools [e.g., @mod_outcomes_2014; @momberg_exposing_2021].

Vegetation surveys were conducted in the summer growing seasons between 2019-2023, wherein the identity and cover of each species in each cell was recorded, and a subset of species were measured for functional traits. The functional trait survey collected traits for many species at the two ends of each grid (to maximise the range of environmental conditions sampled) and sampled more sparsely in the center of the grids. A species was not sampled for functional traits in adjacent cells. Common species were sampled more frequently than rare species. The following traits were measured (following the standardised methods of @perez-harguindeguy_new_2013: plant height, leaf area (LA), specific leaf area (SLA) and leaf dry matter content (LDMC). Thirty-five percent of species were measured for traits at least once, with these species comprising 87% of the total vegetation cover.

Eight environmental variables were measured in each cell of each grid: Rock cover was visually estimated as the percent of a cell covered by rocks large enough to impede plant growth. Soil depth was measured by inserting a metal rod of 60 cm length and 8mm diameter into the soil until further penetration was impeded. Soils deeper than 60 cm were assigned a depth of 61 cm. Three soil depth measurements were taken in each cell and the mean calculated. Northness was calculated as the cosine of the aspect of each cell, with the latter recorded in the field using a compass. Slope height was measured as the vertical difference between the highest and lowest point in a cell, and is a measure of slope steepness. Instantaneous soil moisture was measured in each cell more than 24 hours after the last rainfall event, using a handheld time-domain soil moisture meter (FieldScout 300 TDR; Spectrum Technologies, Plainfield, IL, US) at a depth of 7.5 cm. Instantaneous soil temperature was measured at the same time as soil moisture with a handheld soil thermometer. The instantaneous soil moisture and temperature values were adjusted to account for the increase in air temperature over the time of the campaign. Surface heterogeneity was calculated as the standard deviation of elevation in a cell from a digital surface model. The digital surface model reflects the elevation of the earth's surface (not the ground), and is influenced by vegetation, rocks or any object that may lie on top of the soil. The digital surface model was created from high resolution drone imagery captured by a DJI Phantom 4 Pro drone equipped with a 20MP camera with a 1 inch (CMOS) sensor. Imagery was captured in the winter in August 2023, when the biomass of live vegetation and the volume of dried vegetation was at its lowest. Flights were conducted at 20 m above the take-off point, but the distance to the ground varied due to topographic heterogeneity. The digital surface model was created in Agisoft Metashape following a standard photogrammetry workflow.

```{r interpolation statistics}
#environmental data for reverence 
ref <- read.csv("All_data/clean_data/Environmental data/All_Sites_Environmental_Data_OSF.csv") |>

#Cells we lost
lost <- ref |> 
  anti_join(ind, by = "Cell_ID") |> 
  group_by(site) |> 
  summarise(n = n())

###Correlate interpolation with instantaneous####

  tibble() |> 
  #variables we are interested in
  select(Cell_ID:row, soil_moisture_adj_campaign2, soil_moisture_adj_campaign1, 
         soil_temperature_adj_campaign1, soil_temperature_adj_campaign2, rock_cover) |> 
  mutate(across(contains("soil"), as.numeric)) 

###JOin instantaneous and interpolated 
moisture_dat <- inst_micro |> 
  inner_join(ind, by = "Cell_ID") |> 
  drop_na()

```

The mean soil moisture and temperature of the growing season were calculated using readings from Temperature-Moisture-Sensors [TMS, @wild_climate_2019]. Six or seven TMS were placed in each grid, and recorded soil moisture and temperature readings at 8 cm below the soil surface every 15 minutes for one year (12 January 2023 – 21 January 2024). The start of the growing season was defined as the first day after 21 June when the minimum daily temperature of all loggers at a site were above 5℃. The end of the growing season was the first day before 21 June when all loggers at a site had a minimum daily temperature below 5℃. Following these definitions, the growing season was from 23 August to 8 July at the low site, 1 September to 6 June at the mid site, and 10 October to 3 April at the high site. The mean soil moisture and temperature for the growing season was calculated for each logger and interpolated to other cells in the grid. An inverse-distance-weighted interpolation algorithm was used with a power parameter of two. Cells with more than 50% rock cover were not used in the interpolation process if they contained a logger and did not receive an interpolated value if they were without a logger. Following this threshold, `r lost[2,2]` cells were excluded from interpolation at the low site, `r lost[3,2]` cells were excluded from the mid site, and `r lost[1,2]` cells were excluded from the high site. Cross-validation showed that the interpolation algorithm could not predict the soil moisture and temperature equally well in all grids (@tbl-validation-results). However, the interpolated soil moisture and temperature for the growing season correlated well with the instantaneous soil moisture and temperature measurements (pearson correlation coefficient between instantaneous and interpolated soil moisture = `r cor(moisture_dat$soil_moisture_adj_campaign2, moisture_dat$mean_moist_growing_season)`, pearson correlation coefficient between instantaneous and interpolated soil temperature = `r cor(moisture_dat$soil_temperature_adj_campaign2, moisture_dat$mean_T1_growing_season)`).

A principal component analysis was performed to identify the main axes of environmental variation across the three sites (@fig-environmental-PCA), and identified a soil moisture and temperature axis (PC1, explaining 34% of the variation), as well as a soil depth axis (PC2, explaining 17% of the variation). The following variables were selected to test whether fine-scale variation in community assembly is shaped by micro-environmental variation: mean soil temperature of the growing season (hereafter referred to as soil temperature), mean soil moisture of the growing season (hereafter referred to as soil moisture), rock cover, mean soil depth and surface heterogeneity. These variables may affect community assembly in the following ways: Microclimatic temperature and moisture conditions may differ greatly from the macroclimatic conditions, even in open systems such as grasslands. Different microclimates may act as different filters, selecting for plant assemblages with different traits within short distances of one another [@kemppinen_microclimate_2024]. Rock cover and surface heterogeneity may increase the diversity of available niche space, promoting the coexistence of plants with divergent trait syndromes [@vernham_understanding_2023]. Soil depth may be related to higher soil moisture and increased access to soil resources [@price_within-community_2017], and increased opportunity for underground resource partitioning.

## Statistical methods

To investigate community assembly along elevation and micro-environmental gradients, we used a trait-based method to compare observed functional diversity to the functional diversity expected under a scenario of random assembly (following e.g., @scherrer_disentangling_2019; @price_within-community_2017). Rao’s quadratic entropy (RaoQ) was used as a metric of functional diversity and is the sum of the trait dissimilarity between all species pairs within a sample, weighted by the product of their relative abundances. It is calculated as follows:

$$
RaoQ = \sum_{i=1}^{S-1} \sum_{j=1}^{S} d_{ij} \, p_i \, p_j
$$

Where $p_i$ and $p_j$ is the percentage cover of species $i$ and $j$ in a community with a species richness of $s$. $d_{ij}$ is the dissimilarity between each pair of species $i$and $j$, expressed as Euclidean distance [@botta-dukat_raos_2005]. RaoQ was calculated with the FD package [@laliberté2014] using the study-wide mean traits of species. RaoQ was not calculated for 453 cells which had less than 3 species, where species with trait values made up less than 80% of the vascular cover.

A null-model approach was used to determine whether RaoQ was significantly different from the functional diversity expected under random assembly [@gotzenberger_which_2016]. Null models are a useful tool to gain insight into community assembly processes, but they differ in their ability to detect different assembly mechanisms. Thus, an appropriate null model must be chosen to test each different assembly mechanism. Here, we followed the recommendations of @gotzenberger_which_2016 and selected the C5 null model to test for environmental filtering, and the C2 null model to test for limiting similarity (@fig-nullmodel). We used both null models to test how assembly mechanisms vary along elevation and micro-environmental gradients. The C5 null model shuffles the occurrences of each species across cells, such that the richness of each cell, the frequency of species, and species total cover stays the same as in the observed matrix. The total vegetation cover within cells, and the identity of species occurring in each cell are allowed to deviate from the observed matrix. Thus, we can determine whether the composition of a cell is random compared to a scenario where species can occur in any cell, after controlling for richness and the commonness (frequency in the matrix and total cover) of species. This null model is appropriate to detect environmental filtering because it allows species to occur in cells where they are not present in the observed dataset and has a low type I error rate [@gotzenberger_which_2016]. We built two categories of C5 null model algorithms: The "C5 entire pool model" selected species from the entire species pool to fill the null matrix. Thus, species exclusive to one site in the observed matrix can occur at any site in the null matrix (@fig-nullmodel). This model is appropriate to detect differences in environmental filtering between sites, in other words, filtering by macroclimatic differences at the scale of the elevation gradient. In the "C5 site pool model" we restricted the species pool that the null model fills the matrix from to the site-level species pool (@fig-nullmodel). This model is appropriate to detect environmental filtering at the scale of one site, allowing us to determine whether micro-environmental conditions act as an additional filter after the effect of macroclimate.

The C2 null model shuffles the cover values of species in cells, keeping the richness and total cover of cells constant (@fig-nullmodel). The frequency and total cover of species, and the identity of species in each cell are allowed to deviate from the observed matrix. In this null model, the link between a species' mean trait value and its abundance is not maintained. Species' traits are understood to be linked to their competitive ability and abundance. Thus, this null model test whether assembly is random compared to a community where species' traits do not determine their abundance, while controlling for the total vegetation cover and richness of cells [@gotzenberger_which_2016]. In other words, this null model asks whether the observed community is similar to one where co-occurring, abundant species may have similar or weakly competitive traits. It is recommended that the effect of environmental filtering be removed when testing for limiting similarity [@gotzenberger_which_2016], therefore, we only built a C2 algorithm that selects species from the site-level species pool (@fig-nullmodel). This null model is appropriate to test whether there are differences in limiting similarity between sites, only considering the species that have passed through the macroclimate filter. It is also appropriate to test whether there are differences in similarity between the cells at each site.

To determine whether functional diversity is higher or lower than expected from random assembly, we calculated the standard effect size [SES, @gotelli2002] of RaoQ as a measure of deviance between the observed matrix and null model. SES is calculated as:

$$
SES = (RaoQ_{observed} - \mu{RaoQ_{null}})/\sigma{RaoQ_{null}}
$$

Where $RaoQ_{observed}$ is the observed RaoQ in a cell; $\mu{RaoQ_{null}}$ is the mean of RaoQ from 999 null models, and $\sigma{RaoQ_{null}}$ is the standard deviation of RaoQ from 999 null models. If SES \>0, functional diversity is higher than expected under null assembly, and it is interpreted as a signal of limiting similarity. If SES \< 0, functional diversity is lower than expected under null assembly, and it is interpreted as a signal of habitat filtering. SES was calculated for plant height, LA, SLA and LDMC, using the C5 entire pool model, the C5 site pool model and the C2 site pool model to investigate the effect of elevation and micro-environmental conditions on community assembly.

To determine whether community assembly varies with elevation, linear mixed-effect models were used with the SES of each trait from the C5 entire pool model and C2 site pool model as response variables, and elevation as a predictor. To determine whether micro-environmental variables were related to fine-scale variation in community assembly, separate linear mixed-effect models were built for each trait and each site. The SES of each trait from the C5 site pool model and the C2 site pool model were the response variables, and the following micro-environmental measurements were included as predictors: soil temperature, soil moisture, rock cover, mean soil depth and surface heterogeneity. Predictor variables were standardised to a mean of zero and unit variance prior to modelling. In all analyses, grid was added as a random effect, and a spherical correlation structure was used to account for the spatial autocorrelation between the cells of each grid. To improve the distribution of the model residuals, SES was calculated with the natural log of height, LDMC, and LA in the elevation model, and the natural log of LDMC in the micro-environmental model. Modelling was performed using the nlme package [@pinheiro2025].

To investigate the direction in which traits are filtered, the community-weighted mean (CWM) traits of each cell was calculated with the FD package [@laliberté2014]. A linear mixed effect model with grid as a random effect and a spherical correlation structure was used to determine how CWM varies with elevation. All analyses were performed in R 4.5.2 [@rcoreteam2025].

```{r setup chunk}
traitlist <- c("SLA",  "log_Height", "log_LDMC", "log_LA")

C5_SES_ele_summary <- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C5_SES_ele_summary) = traitlist

C5_SES_ele_Rsq<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C5_SES_ele_Rsq) = traitlist

C5_SES_ele_anova<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C5_SES_ele_anova) = traitlist

C5_SES_ele_cld<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C5_SES_ele_cld) = traitlist

for (t in 1:length(traitlist)) {
  modeldat <-  C5_ele_comb |> 
    filter(trait == traitlist[t]) |> 
    drop_na()
  
  
  model<- lme(SES ~ elevation ,
                  random = ~1|grid, 
                  correlation = corSpher(form = ~ x_coord + y_coord|grid, nugget = TRUE), #spherical structure
                  data = modeldat) #only gaussian family possible
  
  #emmeans and letters
  em_model <- emmeans(model, specs = "elevation", type = "response")
  comp_letters <-cld(em_model, Letters = letters, adjust = "Tukey", sort = FALSE)
  
  #Also save results in a list object so we can call it with quarto
  C5_SES_ele_summary[[t]] <- summary(model)
  C5_SES_ele_Rsq[[t]] <- r.squaredGLMM(model)
  C5_SES_ele_anova[[t]] <- anova(model)
  C5_SES_ele_cld[[t]] <- comp_letters
  
}
rm(model, modeldat) #remove to make sure we don't carry the wrong object over

###Using the logged traits are generally better for model diagnostics than the raw traits
```

# Results

`r C5_ele_comb |>  filter(trait == "log_Height") |> drop_na() |> summarise(n = n())` cells were included in testing how community assembly varies with elevation. `r C5_ele_comb|> filter(trait == "log_Height", site == "GG") |> drop_na() |> summarise(n = n())` Cells were from the low site, `r C5_ele_comb |> filter(trait == "log_Height", site == "WH") |> drop_na() |> summarise(n = n())` cells were from the mid site, and `r C5_ele_comb |> filter(trait == "log_Height", site == "BK") |> drop_na() |> summarise(n = n())` cells were from the high site. All traits at all elevations showed stronger than expected trait convergence with the C5 entire pool null model, except for plant height and LDMC at the high site (@fig-SES-elevation-ridges). However, the C2 site pool null model didn't detect higher than expected trait divergence for any trait at any elevation (@fig-SES-elevation-ridges). Therefore, environmental filtering was the dominant assembly mechanism for all traits at all elevations. No trait followed the trend predicted by the SDH. Leaf area was structured by environmental filtering at all elevations, with no difference in the strength of environmental filtering (@fig-SES-elevation-ridges) or trait diversity (@fig-RaoQ-elevation-ridges) between sites. The environmental filtering of plant height and LDMC became weaker with elevation (@fig-SES-elevation-ridges), while the diversity of plant height and LDMC increased (@fig-RaoQ-elevation-ridges). The assembly of SLA showed a hump-shaped relationship with elevation, with environmental filtering being weakest, and trait diversity being highest at the mid site (@fig-SES-elevation-ridges, @fig-RaoQ-elevation-ridges).

Plant height was generally filtered toward shorter plants with elevation (@fig-CWM-elevation-ridges), but the diversity of plant height increased with elevation (@fig-RaoQ-elevation-ridges), showing the existence of very short as well as very tall plants in the alpine. The community weighted means of leaf area, SLA and LDMC didn't show a linear relationship with altitude, with communities at the mid site having larger leaves and less conservative resource-use strategies than at the high and low site (@fig-CWM-elevation-ridges).

```{r}
#| label: fig-CWM-elevation-ridges
#| fig-cap: Community-weighted mean (CWM) traits of plant height (cm), leaf area (LA, mm$^2$), leaf dry matter content (LDMC, mg.g$^-1$), and specific leaf area (SLA, mm$^2$.mg$^-1$) at the low, mid and high elevation. #| warning: false

#import trait and abundance data
abun_matrix <-read.csv("All_data/comm_assembly_results/abun_matrix.csv", row.names = 1)

mean_traits <- read.csv("All_data/comm_assembly_results/mean_traits.csv", row.names = 1) |> 
  mutate(log_Height = log(Height_cm), 
         log_LA = log(Leaf_area_mm2), 
         log_LDMC = log(LDMC)) |> #use the same log variables as we do in the models
  select(!c(LDMC, Leaf_area_mm2, Height_cm, Thickness_mm))


#compute CWM of each trait for each cell
library(FD)
cwm <- functcomp(x = mean_traits, a = as.matrix(abun_matrix))
cwm2 <- cwm |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "cellref") |> 
  rename(Cell_ID = cellref)  |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = c("log_Height", "log_LDMC", "log_LA", "SLA"), names_to = "trait", values_to = "cwm_value")

cwm_comb <- pos |> 
  #join, one row in env matches many rows in cell_ses due to it containing ses of different traits
  inner_join(cwm2, by = "Cell_ID", relationship = "one-to-many") 


####model CWM ~ elevation####
traitlist <- c("log_Height", "log_LDMC", "log_LA", "SLA")
#lists to store results in
CWM_ele_cld<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(CWM_ele_cld) = traitlist

for (t in 1:length(traitlist)) {
  modeldat <-  cwm_comb |> 
    filter(trait == traitlist[t]) |> 
    mutate(elevation = as.factor(elevation), 
           grid = as.factor(grid)) |> 
    drop_na()
  
  
  model<- lme(cwm_value ~ elevation ,
                  random = ~1|grid, 
                  correlation = corSpher(form = ~ x_coord + y_coord|grid, nugget = TRUE), #spherical structure
                  data = modeldat) #only gaussian family possible
  
  em_model <- emmeans(model, specs = "elevation", type = "response")
  comp_letters <-cld(em_model, Letters = letters, adjust = "Tukey", sort = FALSE)

  #Also save results in a list object so we can call it with quarto
  CWM_ele_cld[[t]] <- comp_letters
}

##Graph####
l1 <- c("log_Height" = "Plant~height", "SLA" = "SLA", "log_LDMC" = "LDMC", "log_LA" = "LA")
cwm_ridges_letters <- data.frame(trait = c(rep("log_Height", 3), rep("SLA", 3), rep("log_LDMC", 3),rep("log_LA", 3)), 
                             elevation = as.factor(c(rep(c("2000", "2500", "3000"), 4))),

  filter(trait %in% c("log_Height", "SLA", "log_LDMC", "log_LA")) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = cwm_value, y = elevation)) +

  theme(legend.position = "none", axis.title = element_text(size = 18),

        strip.background = element_blank(),

cwm_ridges
```

Micro-environmental factors were weakly related to fine-scale variation in community assembly, with relationships varying between traits and sites. The models had low explanatory power with marginal R\$\^2\$ values generally below 0.1 (@tbl-R2-models-C5, @tbl-R2-models-C2), although the models for leaf area (marginal R\$\^2\$, C5 site pool model = 0.333, marginal R\$\^2\$, C2 site pool model = 0.275) and plant height (marginal R\$\^2\$, C5 site pool model = 0.143, marginal R\$\^2\$, C2 site pool model = 0.127) at the low site had better explanatory power. Only surface heterogeneity had a somewhat consistent relationship with community assembly, often being related to higher than expected trait divergence (in 5 out of 12 trait x site combinations, @fig-allsites-microenv_C5_C2), although this relationship was not detected at all sites or for all traits. Other micro-environmental factors had weak and inconsistent effects on community assembly. For example, rock cover was significantly related to limiting similarity in 1 out of 12 trait x site combinations, but was not significantly related to assembly patterns in any other trait (@fig-allsites-microenv_C5_C2). Soil depth was significantly related to limiting similarity in 6 trait x site combinations, but significantly related to environmental filtering in 3 trait x site combinations (@fig-allsites-microenv_C5_C2).

# Discussion

Some preliminary ideas:

Environmental filtering dominant assembly mechanism, not consistently increasing in strength with elevation. Mid site shows unexpected deviation to less conservative, larger leafed species. This could be due to relaxation of environmental filters here, or because of strong competition selecting for more acquisitive (competitive?) traits.

Micro-environmental variables only weakly influence community assembly, and do not have consistent effects. This suggests that assembly at this scale is largely neutral, despite large differences in micro-environmental conditions?

Perhaps missing: An analysis or figure showing the extent of environmental variation present here?

Grid number is the unique ID of each grid in each site.Number of loggers are the number of TMS loggers used to create the interpolated temperature or moisture surface. $R^2$ is the squared Pearson correlation coefficient between the observed and interpolated temperature or moisture value. The root mean square error is the square root of the mean squared difference between observed and interpolated values in the grid. The bias is the mean of the differences between observed and interpolated values in the grid.
```{r}
#| message: false

#import validation results

  group_by(site, grid_number, variable) |> 
  summarise(
    n        = n(),
    R2       = ifelse(var(observed) > 0, 
                      cor(observed, predicted)^2, NA_real_),
    RMSE     = sqrt(mean(error^2)),
    bias     = mean(error),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |> 
  mutate(site = case_when(site == "BK" ~ "high", 
                          site == "WH" ~ "mid", 
                          site == "GG" ~ "low"), 
         site = factor(site, levels = c("low", "mid", "high")), 
         variable = case_when(variable == "mean_T1_growing_season" ~ "mean soil temperature", 
                              variable == "mean_moist_growing_season" ~ "mean soil moisture")) |> 
  arrange(variable, site, grid_number) |> 
  flextable() |> 
  colformat_double(j = 4:6, digits = 3) |> 
  set_header_labels(site = "Site", 
                    grid_number = "Grid number", 
                    variable = "Variable", 
                    n = "Number of loggers", 
                    R2 = "R\u00B2", 
                    RMSE = "Root mean square error",
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-nullmodel
#| fig-cap: "The different null models used here, and how to interepret their results. To test the SDH, the C5 entire pool model and the C2 site pool model is used. The C5 entire pool model shuffles cover values accross cells, keeping species richness of cells, species frequency and species total cover constant. If SES<0 calculated with the C5 null model, we interpret it as a signal of environmental filtering. SES>0 indicates that no environmental filtering effect is present. The C2 site pool model shuffles cover values accross species, but only accorss the species that occur at the site in the observed species by site matrix. The richness and total vascular cover of cells are kept constant. SES>0 from this null model indicates that limiting similarity is present, while SES<0 shows no evidence of limiting similarity. The SDH predicts that community assembly will shift from limiting similarity to environmental filtering with elevation, thus that SES values should decrease with elevation. To test whether micro-environmental conditions affect community assembly within sites, the C2 site pool model and C5 site pool model are used. The C5 site pool model shuffles cover values across the cells in each site, so that a species unique to one site may not occur in another site. SES<0 from this null model indicates environmental filtering, while a SES>0 does not give evidence of environmental filtering. We expect micro-environmental conditions to have a negative or positive linear relationship with SES."
knitr::include_graphics("C:\\Users\\imke6\\Documents\\PhD 2025\\Ch1 Drakensberg analysis community assembly\\Ch2_write_up\\null model figure.png")
```
